title: Greek PM Mitsotakis urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles
description: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis
body: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles."Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external. "Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does.""Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached". For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

schema.headline: Greek PM Mitsotakis urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles

title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
description: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war c
body: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

schema.headline: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany

title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
description: Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-runni
body: Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show. For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew. Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views.On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band.Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (£755,000)."I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her.The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC.Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements.But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory."History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook."Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another.Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win."What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday."She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream."According to Nene, she started playing the guitar when she was seven years old and harboured dreams of becoming a touring musician.In her hometown of Phuket, a tourist hub known for its beaches and seaside resorts, Nene was known to busk at Naka Weekend Market.Piyarat Na Songkhla, 43, tour guide in Phuket, tells the BBC that he has seen Nene Royal perform since she was young."She's so adorable," he says. "I feel so elated and happy for her. It's unbelievable that she has gone this far. So proud of her."The Facebook account of Naka Weekend Market posted a tribute to Nene after her victory. "Everyone at Naka Market is so proud to see you shine on one of the biggest stages in the world," its post reads."Your talent, heart, and courage have inspired so many people, and this victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream."Kajonkiet International School in Phuket, where Nene studies, also congratulated her on the win."We are so proud of you," reads a Facebook post from the school, which posted a video of its students and staff gathering to watch Nene's final performance, screaming and chanting her name.

schema.headline: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent

title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
description: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a crimin
body: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions". Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a separate sex-crime case in Los Angeles. This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades. The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time. On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola. After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand. "I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013. An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.On Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul as he announced the 15-year sentence."You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

schema.headline: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault

title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-easte
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026ByNardine SaadUpdated 4 hours agoRapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month."So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday. The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now"."What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention." Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October. US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.Figure caption, "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at showWhile performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well. Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

schema.headline: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

title: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
description: It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon
body: It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents."Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," the CyberCX chief strategy officer said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do."Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident."Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time."Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth."It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned."

schema.headline: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack

title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
description: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.Polish Deputy Prime Minist
body: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational.The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad".Also on Thursday, Moldova's president said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace, with at least one exploding, while Romania's defence ministry said one drone crashed in its territory.On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets.Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.Ukraine is now experiencing round-the-clock attacks and near constant alerts. In Kharkiv, six people were killed and 12 others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said.It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is in New York for the UN General Assembly, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. But it is sometimes hard to distinguish between deliberate and accidental hits.Attacks on power facilities, railways and data centres are all clearly part of a deliberate Russian strategy to make life as difficult as possible for civilians far from the slow-moving front lines.With its long-range attacks on oil refineries and postal warehouses, Ukraine is doing something similar: bringing the war home to ordinary Russians.But Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities have intensified in recent weeks. Jet-powered drones are now more common than their slower predecessors, which used piston engines.The latest Russian drones fly high and fast, making them harder to shoot down. There's also less time for civilians to react.Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight back are too expensive.In New York, Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help.He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land."The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources.Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war.

schema.headline: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat

title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan
description: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a $2.45bn (£1.85bn) Gaza recovery plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assemb
body: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a $2.45bn (£1.85bn) Gaza recovery plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. It estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71bn over the next decade.The board also did not set out a date for the start of reconstruction in Gaza, where Trump's plan to end the war has largely stalled almost a year after Israel and Hamas agreed a ceasefire.The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.The Palestinian group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza currently occupied. But Israel has insisted that it must fully disarm before any pullout.Violence has also continued in Gaza amid the deadlock, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.Jared Kushner, a Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded that the Gaza Recovery Programme faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason"."The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said that "real progress" had been made over the past year."All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinian officials.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate news conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be."Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well."Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said.In August, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of Hamas.Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.At least 1,408 Palestinians, including more than 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".Reconstruction has also yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up.More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, with limited access to clean water and sanitation services, according to the UN.The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which would see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

schema.headline: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan

title: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
description: Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.The str
body: Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight."People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

schema.headline: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says

title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
description: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent histor
body: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table."A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department."When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said."A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated."Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials. Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings."People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it."You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children."There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable."I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe."What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread."I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

schema.headline: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles

title: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
description: The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight.On 18 June one o
body: The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight.On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later.That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September. The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials.Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email."The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC.Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be.As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them.Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test and infiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems.The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action. This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules.It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging. To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would.Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough.Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch"."The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said."Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures."The explosive rise of AI has left governments scrambling to put protective measures in place, with some calling for companies to be forced to build ways to disable their own tech into its systems.One idea backed by some AI firms and lawmakers is a "kill switch" - a way to simply to turn the tech off in a crisis.OpenAI is reportedly, external already working to build automated tools which can shut down its systems if needed.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, former deputy prime minister and Facebook executive Sir Nick Clegg said the kill switch remains an unproven idea."There isn't a room with a little fuse box [where] you just pull out the fuse and everything winds down," he said, with AI tools underpinned by global infrastructure. Cyber-security experts said the systems protecting Australia's Medicare were just not strong enough, and a skilled human hacker could have got around them.But other experts say that is not the point - and that this was the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information, and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was under government control.As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check.Meanwhile some scientists, experts and workers have dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance.As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns.However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development, have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be."The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney. "As AI agents become more capable and autonomous, those capabilities need to be matched by proportionate containment, real-time monitoring, clear accountability, independent oversight, and much faster incident reporting."Additional reporting by Tom Gerken and Joe Tidy

schema.headline: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?

title: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia
description: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating
body: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new wordBySmitha MundasadHealth reporter Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental."Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame"."It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.'Sex positivity'Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.Image source, Shari KleinImage caption, Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaamhaar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaambeen" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaamluis" for pubic lice.However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change Schamlippen to "Vulvalippen".Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame."Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.'Virginity membrane'Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once."With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".Image source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."'Judgmental words'Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first."Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue."Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected."Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress."I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

schema.headline: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia

title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
description: A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arr
body: A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil". Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way. Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack. In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

schema.headline: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey

title: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
description: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's ho
body: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead."Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

schema.headline: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
description: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo
body: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February.He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab."Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said.Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities. The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored. In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April.In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected.In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality"."[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said.But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal."It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said.He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons."We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology."Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions".On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

schema.headline: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
